body: We work with local partners to protect saiga habitat, strengthen protection on the ground, and support community-led conservation across the species’ range.

hero.title: Who we are
hero.intro: An alliance of researchers, rangers, communities and supporters working for the recovery of the saiga antelope.

mission.statement: To secure the long-term survival of the saiga antelope across its range, and to keep the steppe grasslands it depends on healthy and connected.
mission.body: We work towards a future in which saiga herds move freely across the steppe, in which the people who live alongside them benefit from that recovery, and in which the decisions affecting both are made with evidence and with local knowledge.

approach.title: Conservation built with the people of the steppe.
body: The Saiga Conservation Alliance brings together field scientists, protected area staff, community organisations and supporters across the saiga’s range. We are small by design: most of what we do is delivered through long-standing local partnerships rather than by parachuting teams into landscapes they do not know.

That means our work looks different in each country we operate in — but the intent is the same everywhere. Keep herds safe, keep the grasslands intact, and keep the people who live alongside saigas at the centre of the decisions that affect them.

It also means we work slowly where slow is what the work needs. Village committees, ranger teams and monitoring records all take years to become reliable, and none of them survive being rushed. Where we can move quickly — a small grant to a researcher whose field season is about to be lost — we do.

We are deliberately not the largest organisation working on the steppe, and we do not try to be. Our role is to connect the people who are already there, to fund the work that falls between larger programmes, and to make sure the evidence reaches the people writing policy.

what-is-a-saiga._label: About Saigas — What is a Saiga?

meta.title: What is a Saiga?
meta.description: Meet the saiga antelope — an ancient migratory species of the Eurasian steppe, and why it needs protecting.

hero.title: What is a saiga?
hero.intro: A remarkable antelope. A vital part of the steppe. A species worth protecting.

intro.lead: The saiga is an antelope of the Eurasian steppe, and one of the oldest surviving large mammals in the world — it shared this landscape with mammoths. It is instantly recognisable from its bulbous, downward-facing nose, and almost as instantly forgettable to anyone who has never seen one, which is much of the problem.
intro.body: Saigas live in herds, move long distances between seasonal grazing, and give birth in an extraordinary synchronised burst each spring. Everything about them is built for open grassland: the speed, the migration, the nose that filters summer dust and warms winter air. It is also what makes them so exposed when that grassland is cut up, fenced, or emptied of the herders who have always shared it.

factsheet.title: The saiga at a glance
factsheet.intro: The short answers, in one place — for anyone who wants the facts before the story.

behaviour.title: Built for the steppe
body: Saigas are shaped almost entirely by the demands of open grassland. The distinctive nose warms cold air in winter and filters dust thrown up by moving herds in summer, and their long legs are built for covering distance rather than for cover.

They form large herds and undertake long seasonal migrations in search of food and water. Calving is highly synchronised — most calves in a population are born within a week — which is both a remarkable survival strategy and a moment of extreme vulnerability.

distribution.title: Where saigas live
body: Almost all the world’s wild saigas live in Kazakhstan, across the vast steppe and semi-desert of the country’s centre and west. Smaller populations survive in Mongolia, in the Russian Federation, and in Uzbekistan, where herds cross seasonally from neighbouring range states.

Within those countries, saigas are not evenly spread. Herds concentrate where grazing and water allow, which means a large share of a national population can occupy a comparatively small area at certain times of year — most dramatically at calving, when tens of thousands of animals gather in a matter of days.

They also move. Seasonal migrations of several hundred kilometres are routine, and the routes shift year to year with rainfall and disturbance. Protecting saigas therefore means protecting a landscape rather than a place: the grazing, the water, and the corridors that join them.
distribution.caption: Saiga populations are concentrated in Kazakhstan, with smaller populations in Mongolia, Uzbekistan and the Russian Federation.

meta.title: Why Saigas Matter
meta.description: The ecological, cultural and global significance of the saiga antelope.

hero.title: Why saigas matter
hero.intro: A grazing species that shapes the grassland, and a cultural presence far older than any border on the map.

why-saigas-matter.intro: Saigas are not simply a species that happens to live on the steppe — they are part of how the steppe works, and part of how the people there understand where they live. Losing them would mean losing a functioning grassland and a piece of cultural memory at the same time.

blocks.title: A keystone of the grassland
body: Grazing by large herds prevents any single plant community from dominating, maintaining the mosaic of grasses and herbs that a healthy steppe depends on. Where saigas disappear, that mosaic simplifies — and with it goes much of the wider biodiversity the grassland supports.
Their long-distance movements carry nutrients and seeds across landscapes that would otherwise be far more fragmented. Few other species on the steppe operate at that scale, and none can replace it.

Saigas are also prey. Wolves, foxes, eagles and scavenging birds all depend to some degree on a species that arrives in numbers and moves on again, and a steppe without saigas is a thinner place for all of them.

blocks.title: Older than any border on the map
body: Saigas appear in the folklore, songs and decorative traditions of communities across the range, and in petroglyphs that predate every state now responsible for protecting them. They are part of how the steppe is described by the people who live in it.
That memory is not evenly held. In places where herds have been absent for a generation, younger people may never have seen one, and the species survives locally as a story rather than as an animal.

Where saigas do return, they carry a good deal with them. Communities that once counted their disappearance as a loss now count their recovery as something achieved locally — which is a far more durable basis for conservation than any external programme.

summary.title: A species worth keeping
summary.body: The case for saigas is not sentimental. They hold a grassland ecosystem together, they connect landscapes that human infrastructure keeps dividing, and they matter to the communities who share the steppe with them. A species that has survived since the Pleistocene has now come within a decade of disappearing twice in living memory — and both times, it was people who turned it around.

meta.title: Population History & Threats
meta.description: How saiga numbers have changed over time, and the pressures the species still faces.

hero.title: Population history & threats
hero.intro: From millions, to near collapse, to a fragile recovery — and the pressures that remain.

population-history-and-threats.intro: Within living memory the saiga has gone from one of the most numerous large mammals on earth to a species reduced by more than ninety per cent, and back again to a recovering population. That volatility is the defining feature of saiga conservation: numbers can move faster than policy can respond.

history.title: How we got here
history.intro: Four broad phases, rather than a year-by-year record — the detail changes by country, but the shape of it does not.

items.title: Near collapse
items.body: Sustained hunting across the range reduces saiga numbers to a few thousand animals, and the species disappears entirely from large parts of its former range.

items.title: Soviet-era recovery
items.body: Strict hunting controls and a managed harvest allow numbers to recover to well over a million animals, in what remains one of the largest recoveries of any large mammal.

items.title: Post-Soviet collapse
items.body: The breakdown of state protection and a sharp rise in illegal hunting for horn cut the global population by more than ninety per cent within a decade.

items.title: Mass mortality
items.body: A bacterial die-off removes a large share of one recovering population within weeks, a reminder that recovery is never secure on its own.

items.title: A fragile recovery
items.body: Sustained protection, particularly of calving grounds, has allowed numbers to rise again — though the population remains concentrated, and concentrated populations remain vulnerable.

graph.title: Estimated global saiga population over time
graph.intro: Saiga numbers have changed dramatically over time, with periods of steep decline followed by strong recovery. This graph shows the combined total across all five populations, which can hide the fact that some remain much smaller than others.
graph.captionHtml:
Covers the five major saiga populations: Ustyurt, Betpak-Dala, Ural, Northwest Pre-Caspian, and Mongolia.
Source: CMS COP9 II/6 historical population estimates; CMS Saiga MOS5 Overview Report (2025).

threats.title: The threats saigas face
threats.intro: Rarely one at a time. Most of the losses of the last century came from two or more of these arriving together.

items.title: Human-wildlife conflict
items.body: Saigas share the steppe with livestock and the people who depend on it. Where grazing, water and space are contested, wildlife is easily seen as a cost rather than an asset.

items.title: Poaching and illegal trade
items.body: Demand for horn continues to drive illegal hunting, and because only males carry horns it can skew the sex ratio of a population far beyond the number of animals killed.

items.title: Disease
items.body: Mass mortality events can remove a large share of a population within weeks. The triggers are still not fully understood, which makes prevention extremely difficult.

items.title: Climate and extreme weather
items.body: Severe winters and long droughts both hit saigas hard, and a changing climate is making the extremes that herds cannot walk away from more frequent.

items.title: Barriers to movement
items.body: Roads, railways, fencing and border infrastructure can cut herds off from the seasonal grazing and water they need, turning a long migration into a dead end.

summary.title: Recovery is not the end of it
summary.body: Saiga numbers are higher today than at any point since the collapse of the 1990s, and that is genuinely worth saying. But the population remains concentrated, the threats have not gone away, and this species has twice shown how quickly a good count can become a bad one. What holds a recovery in place is unglamorous and continuous: patrols through the calving season, monitoring that does not stop when the funding cycle does, and communities with a reason to want herds on their land.

meta.title: Saiga Policy & Protection
meta.description: Legal status, international agreements and the protection framework for saigas.

hero.title: Saiga policy & protection
hero.intro: The agreements, laws and enforcement that stand between the saiga and another collapse.

policy-and-protection.intro: Protecting a species that crosses international borders means protection has to cross them too. Saiga conservation rests on a framework of national law, regional cooperation and international agreement — and on the enforcement capacity to make any of it real on the ground.

items.name: Convention on Migratory Species (CMS)
body: The saiga is listed under the Convention on Migratory Species, the international treaty concerned with animals that cross national borders. Under it, range states have agreed a shared Memorandum of Understanding and a work programme for saiga conservation.

In practice this is what makes range-wide planning possible: it gives the countries involved a common set of objectives, a schedule for reporting against them, and a forum in which problems that cross borders can be raised as shared problems rather than someone else's.

items.name: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES)
body: CITES governs international trade in saiga products, principally horn. The species is listed on Appendix II, which means commercial international trade is permitted only under strict conditions and with export permits from the country of origin.

The listing matters because demand for horn is what drove the collapse of the 1990s and continues to drive illegal hunting today. CITES gives enforcement agencies a legal basis for acting on seizures, and gives range and consumer states a common vocabulary for the trade they are trying to control.

national.title: National protection
body: Each range state protects saigas in its own law. Hunting is banned outright across the range, protected areas cover key calving grounds and wintering areas, and penalties for possession and trafficking of horn have been strengthened in most range states over the past decade.

The binding constraint is rarely the law itself but the capacity to apply it: patrol coverage across enormous areas, evidence handling that stands up in court, coordination between agencies on either side of a border, and the resources available to the people responsible for all of it.

callout.title: How the system fits together
callout.body: International agreement sets the direction, national law makes it enforceable, and rangers make it real. Each layer depends on the one below it — which is why much of SCA’s policy work is translation: turning commitments made in meeting rooms into funded patrols, trained teams and equipment that actually arrives.

meta.title: Donor Tours
meta.description: Join a small group of supporters in saiga country and meet the teams behind the work.

hero.title: Donor tours
hero.intro: See the steppe for yourself. A small number of supporters travel with us each year to meet the people doing the work, in the places where it happens.

donor-tours.intro: A donor tour is time spent in saiga country with the rangers, researchers, teachers and herders who work there all year. Groups are deliberately small, the dates follow the season rather than the calendar, and every place taken helps fund the work you have come to see.

blocks.title: Time in the field, not on a coach
body: Tours are built around whatever the season allows: a calving-ground survey in spring, a ranger patrol in the summer pastures, an afternoon in a village school that has run a saiga club for years. Nothing is staged for visitors.

Days are long and conditions are simple. Accommodation is usually a field camp or a guesthouse in a small town, travel is by 4x4 over open ground, and the weather on the steppe decides a good deal of the itinerary.
In return, you spend your time with the people who know the landscape best, and you see the work as it actually is rather than as a report describes it.

blocks.title: Small groups, planned well ahead
body: Each tour takes a small group and is arranged with our partners in the range state months in advance, so that a visit adds to the work rather than interrupting it.
We will talk through visas, permits, travel insurance, fitness and the realities of remote fieldwork before anyone commits, and trips can be adjusted where health or mobility needs it.
Costs cover travel, accommodation and local guiding, with a contribution to SCA's programmes. We set out exactly what that contribution supports before you book.

summary.title: Register your interest
summary.body: Tours are announced to supporters first, and places usually go quickly. Tell us you would like to hear about the next one and we will be in touch with dates, costs and what the trip involves as soon as they are set.
